title: Arctic Sea Ice Keeps Shrinking and Getting Thinner
summary:
Every year, the frozen seawater covering the Arctic Ocean grows during the long, dark winter and shrinks during the warmer months. It usually reaches its largest size in March and its smallest in September. Satellites have tracked this cycle since late 1978, giving scientists nearly 50 years of measurements.

Those measurements show the ice is shrinking at both ends of the cycle. In 2026, Arctic sea ice reached its smallest size on September 12, covering about 4.6 million square kilometers, or 1.78 million square miles. According to NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center, that tied 2008, 2010 and 2025 for the 10th-lowest level in the satellite record. The smallest ever was in September 2012. In winter, the March 2026 peak tied March 2025 for the lowest winter maximum on record.

Every summer from 2007 through 2026 ranks among the 20 lowest in the record. But over the past decade, the summer low has stayed fairly steady instead of dropping quickly. NASA researchers say more clouds over the Arctic in recent years blocked some sunlight and helped limit melting. Still, summer ice remains far below its historical average.

The ice itself is also changing. In the past, much of the Arctic held thick "multiyear ice," which survives at least one summer. Now more of the Arctic is covered by thinner ice that forms in a single winter and melts more easily.

Natural weather patterns affect the ice from year to year, but scientists say they cannot fully explain the long decline. Rising global temperatures, together with natural changes, have contributed to the loss. Scientists project the Arctic Ocean could become nearly ice-free in summer at least once before 2050.

Satellites with special microwave sensors let scientists see the ice even through clouds.
why_it_matters: Arctic sea ice is a key part of Earth's climate system, and its long decline shows how rising temperatures are changing a region that has had ice cover for thousands of years.

background_read: Sea ice is frozen ocean water that floats on the surface, unlike icebergs, which break off glaciers on land.
Bright white ice reflects much of the sunlight that hits it, while dark open ocean absorbs more heat.
When sea ice melts, more dark water is exposed, which can warm the region further.
Scientists compare each year with long satellite records to see whether changes are part of a lasting trend.
